generator.params.frond_length.why: A palm's leaf is its frond, petiole and all, drawn as long as its flora gives it.

generator.params.fan.why: A fan palm's frond ends in a fan of segments; a feather palm's bears leaflets along its rachis.

generator.params.petiole.why: A fan palm's blade stands at the end of a petiole about half the frond's length (the built-in cabbage, saw and fan palms, 0.45 to 0.54); a feather palm's leaflets start a short way up (date and royal palms, 0.1 to 0.22).

generator.params.pieces.why: A feather palm's rachis is drawn in many pieces to bear its leaflets; a fan palm's petiole needs few.

generator.params.old_angle.why: Fan palms' old fronds stand out flatter (the built-in fan palms, 72 to 75 degrees from the vertical) than feather palms' arching ones (55 to 62).

generator.params.hang.why: An old fan frond turns further down before it dies than a feather palm's (the built-in species, 35 to 50 against 20 to 25 degrees, short of the most, which hang in a skirt).

generator.params.fan_arch.why: A fan's edge segments droop below its middle, as the built-in cabbage and California fan palms' do (30 to 35 degrees).

generator.params.leaflet_scatter.why: A feather palm's leaflets stand a little above and below the rachis's V, not in two flat planes (the built-in date and royal palms, 15 to 18 degrees; less for most).

generator.params.suckers.why: A clonal palm (Tomlinson's model: stems from the foot of the first) sends up suckers round its foot; a solitary one sends none.

generator.params.petiole_radius.why: A longer frond stands on a stouter petiole and rachis: the built-in palms' are 0.008 to 0.01 of the frond's length in radius (saw palmetto 8 mm on a 1.25 m frond, royal palm 35 mm on 3.5 m).

generator.params.trunk_rate.why: A palm's crown stands about four tenths of a frond's length above its trunk, so its trunk rises to the rest of its usual height over about fifty years.

generator.params.trunk_radius.why: A trunk's radius, a little under half its greatest stated diameter, since a palm's trunk is widest at its foot or its belly.

generator.defaults.trunk_radius.why: Where no diameter is stated, a taller palm stands on a stouter trunk: about 7 mm of radius a metre of greatest height (the built-in royal and date palms, 0.22 to 0.25 m at 25 to 30 m; a 3 m parlour palm about 2 cm).

generator.program.note: The lineage's own program (growth plan G2.3a), on the palm base: it gives the values its species leave unset, which the palm program gave as defaults until then.

generator.defaults.note: Values the palm program leaves to its species, near the middle of the five built-in palms' (date, royal, cabbage, saw and California fan palms), leaning to a feather palm's, since most of the family's genera are feather palms (Mabberley 2017, subfamily V Arecoideae the largest): about a dozen fronds a year, each living two or three years and opening over a year. They yield to any file's values.

growth.note: Grown to sixty years, as the built-in palms are (fifty to sixty).

variants.note: One seed in the open, as the other form defaults.

appearance.note: The built-in palms' colours and cards: a grey trunk, mid-green narrow leaflets, segments folded and drooping as the built-in fan palms' are, a green sheath for a crownshaft, a brown boot.

rules.note: What the palm program's values mean for a palm's stated characters: its frond is its whole leaf; fan or feather from its division pattern, with the petiole, its girth, rachis pieces and frond angles of the built-in fan or feather palms; suckers if it is clonal; the trunk's rise from its usual height less the crown, and its girth from its stated diameter or else its height.

traits.flower_merosity.note: Simpson, Plant Systematics (2019) p. 238, 241: perianth 3+3, rarely 2+2, none or many (Floral Diagrams p. 112: basic pattern trimerous).

traits.hypanthium.note: Simpson, Plant Systematics (2019) p. 238, 505: Simpson calls the flowers hypogynous. Simpson p. 505 defines hypogynous and epigynous as flowers without a hypanthium.

traits.note: Hutchinson (vol. 2, 2nd ed., 1959), family 393 Palmae: stems often clothed in the bases of old leaves, the leaves in a cluster at the top (scattered in climbing palms), whole or divided pinnately or palmately; flowers small and regular, in an often paniculate inflorescence among or below the leaves, with one to many spathes; perianth double, three sepals and three petals; stamens usually 6, rarely many; ovary superior, of three carpels, free or joined; fruit a berry or drupe. The stems' wood is the palms' own, with no secondary growth; they are counted woody, as the floras call them trees.

traits.leaf_habit.note: Watson and Dallwitz, The Families of Flowering Plants (DELTA data, items edited May 2026), family Palmae: how long the leaves last (character 37), coded evergreen. Read from the coded states by script (spec-rework/b1/delta/mapdelta.py with character 21 added); states the authors do not qualify, side by side, read as often.
